cells.tense: You have named a direction and you are looking after what is growing toward it, both at once.
cells.ask: Tell one person what you are growing and what it needs next, then give it that.
cells.core:
You know what you are aiming at, and you are looking after what is growing toward it. They are not two jobs pulling against each other. The aim is what tells you what to water. The care follows from the aim, not the other way around.

It is quieter than it sounds. No drama, no proving, just the daily work of not looking away from either one. What it costs to keep is this: you cannot let the caring go slack and still call it a direction. Say out loud to someone what you are growing and what it needs next. Once it is named where another person can hear it, help arrives at the right spot.
cells.sheetLine: You aim, you tend, and you know which is which.
cells.verb: Settling on a direction and holding to it
cells.place: Looking after what is still growing

cells.tense: You are steering a thing that is still growing as though it were finished and needed you to shape it.
cells.ask: Choose one thing you are growing and leave it alone for a week — no adjusting, no checking, just water it.
cells.core:
You are aiming somewhere real, but you are pushing the aim harder than the growing can take. You can already see where it should end up, so you correct it, nudge it, speed it along. The direction is right. The grip is the problem. The belief underneath is that it will not happen unless you stand over it.

The open space you keep filling in is where things get to be smaller than your picture of them, slower than your plan, shaped a little differently than you intended. That is not failure. That is the thing growing on its own. Let one of them be unfinished for a week, and see what it does without your hand on it.
cells.sheetLine: You are shaping what has not finished growing, and it shows.
cells.verb: Settling on a direction and holding to it
cells.place: Looking after what is still growing

cells.tense: You set a direction once, it did not go the way it needed to, and you stopped pointing anywhere.
cells.ask: Name one thing you are already tending — a habit, a person, a project — and say what it needs today.
cells.core:
The aim is still there. You are just not standing where you can see it. Pointing at something and having it not work out turned into not pointing at all. It is safer to look after whatever is in front of you than to pick a direction again. So what is growing now gets watered, but it does not get aimed anywhere.

This is not about getting inspired again. It is about noticing you are already looking after something — you can name it right now — and letting that care have a direction attached to it. Small is fine. One aim, said out loud to another person, does more than a large one you keep hidden in case it does not work.
cells.sheetLine: You are tending something. You have just stopped saying where it is going.

cells.tense: You are steering and tending both, but you would say the situation is doing it to you.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you did today that shaped what is growing and call it a choice you made.
cells.core:
At its plainest, you can point at the thing you are growing and say, that direction is mine, that care is mine. You know what you chose and what you watered, and you carry both without announcing them. The direction holds because you are standing in it.

Right now you are steering and tending, and it looks like the situation. The seeds you watered, the time you gave, the thing you kept checking on — that is a direction, and it came from you. But you describe it as circumstances. The timing was off, someone needed this, it just happened that way. Maybe all true. Also true: you decided. Pick one thing you shaped today and call it your choice.
cells.sheetLine: You are already choosing what grows. You have not claimed it yet.

The reader could reasonably say 'I don't know what I'm growing, that's the whole problem,' so the asks need to work for someone who never chose the thing they're tending. If I'm wrong about the read, the asks still hold — they ask for a visible act, not a confession of identity. The sentence that serves me more than them is 'You're already deciding what gets to become something,' because it tells them what they are rather than handing them where the pen is.
